---
title: Feature flags
description: What the serde, view, rt-feedback and parallel Cargo features gate, their defaults and how to trim them.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

All features are enabled by default and forwarded to the `sourcier-core`
engine crate. You only configure features on the `sourcier` facade.

| Feature | Default | Gates |
| ------- | ------- | ----- |
| `serde` | yes | `Serialize`/`Deserialize` for maps, positions and `FeedbackSnapshot`; wire-format loading |
| `view` | yes | `LineOffsets`, `view`, `view_str`, `line_offsets`, `position_from_offset`, `offset_from_position`, `display_position` |
| `rt-feedback` | yes | `RuntimeFeedback`, `FeedbackSnapshot`, `with_feedback` on map and builder |
| `parallel` | no | Multi-threaded line-offset index construction with `rayon` |

## What each feature means for your build

`serde` adds the serialization derives and the payload-compatibility logic.
Tools that keep positions only in memory can drop it.

`view` adds the per-file line index (a single `memchr`-accelerated scan, 4
bytes per line) and every byte-extraction and offset-bridge API. Diagnostics
tools almost always keep it; pure id registries can drop it.

`rt-feedback` adds atomic counters behind `Arc<RuntimeFeedback>`. No locks
are taken on the reporting path; the cost when unused is the unused code
path.

`parallel` is opt-in because on a 2-core reference VM the thread-pool
overhead outweighed the scan savings. Enable it on many-core build machines
processing large file sets; it adds the `rayon` dependency.

## Trimming recipes

Keep only byte extraction:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[dependencies]
sourcier = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["view"] }`} />

Keep serialization but no views and no statistics:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[dependencies]
sourcier = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["serde"] }`} />

Enable everything including parallelism:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[dependencies]
sourcier = { version = "2.0", features = ["parallel"] }`} />

<Aside type="caution">
	Disabling a feature removes its APIs from the compiled crate: code that
	calls `view` with `default-features = false` fails to compile. Cargo
	unifies features across your dependency graph, so another crate in the
	tree can re-enable a feature you trimmed.
</Aside>

## MSRV per configuration

The minimum supported Rust version is 1.99 for every feature configuration;
CI verifies `cargo check` across feature combinations.

## Next steps

- Follow <LinkCard title="Installation" href="/guides/installation/" /> for the install commands behind these snippets.
- Follow <LinkCard title="Tuning performance" href="/guides/tuning-performance/" /> when deciding between `parallel` and the default scan.
- Check the <LinkCard title="API surface" href="/reference/api/" /> for the items each feature gates.


---

---
title: Position encoding
description: Stable u64 bit layouts for AbsolutePosition and RelativePosition, the reserved zero encoding, and wire-format compatibility rules.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Positions are stable `u64` encodings. The layout is documented so raw values
can be persisted safely: the layout is part of the public API and stable
across semver-compatible releases. All fields are packed most significant
first, and the end line and end column are inclusive.

## Absolute layout

`AbsolutePosition<Id>` packs five fields. The file id always occupies the
most significant bits, and the remaining fields are laid out so no bits are
wasted:

| Id type | File id | Start line | Start col | End line | End col |
| ------- | -------- | ---------- | --------- | -------- | ------- |
| `u8`    | `56..64` | `40..56`   | `32..40`  | `16..32` | `0..8`  |
| `u16`   | `48..64` | `32..48`   | `24..32`  | `8..24`  | `0..8`  |

Field widths follow from the ranges: lines are `u16` (16 bits), columns are
`u8` (8 bits), and the id field is 8 bits for `u8` and 16 bits for `u16`.

Because the fields are ordered from most to least significant, comparing the
packed values as integers is equivalent to ordering spans lexicographically:
file id first, then start line, start column, end line, end column.

## Relative layout

`RelativePosition` stores no file id and packs into the low 48 bits:

| Field | Bits |
| ----- | ---- |
| Start line | `32..48` |
| Start col | `24..32` |
| End line | `8..24` |
| End col | `0..8` |

The high 16 bits are always zero. `RelativePosition::from_raw` masks them
away, so values with garbage in the high bits still round-trip losslessly.

## Reserved encodings

Ids are one-based: the first file in a map receives id `1`, and `0` is never
assigned. This keeps the all-zero encoding reserved for future use as a
sentinel:

- `AbsolutePosition::from_raw` returns `None` when the embedded file id is
  `0`, for both id types.
- `RelativePosition::from_raw` masks the high bits and accepts the all-zero
  value; use `try_new` if you need range validation on rebuild.

## Limits

| Field | Width | Limit | Exceeding it |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ------------ |
| Files per map (`u8` ids) | 8 bits | 255 files | `MapError::TooManyFiles { max: 255 }` |
| Files per map (`u16` ids) | 16 bits | 65,535 files | `MapError::TooManyFiles { max: 65535 }` |
| Line numbers | 16 bits | 65,535 lines | Offset conversion returns `None` |
| Columns | 8 bits | 255 byte columns | Offset conversion returns `None` |
| File size for line indexes | 32-bit offsets | 4 GiB | `MapError::FileTooLarge { size }` |

Columns are byte columns, not character columns: a multi-byte UTF-8 character
counts one column per byte.

## Wire format

With the `serde` feature, `SourceFilesMap` serializes to a payload that
carries only the raw entries and the phase flag; the lookup state is derived
from the sorted entries and rebuilt on load. This keeps payloads compact —
roughly half the 1.0 lookup-state memory.

Backward compatibility:

- 2.0 payloads rebuild the verified path index on load.
- 1.0 payloads that still carry the redundant `path_to_id` table deserialize
  without error; the redundant field is ignored.

`AbsolutePosition`, `RelativePosition` and `FeedbackSnapshot` serialize as
their raw forms with the default `serde` feature, and round trips preserve
the bits exactly.

<Aside type="caution">
	Raw `u64` values are safe to persist only within one semver-compatible
	release line of the encoding. The layout is documented and stable, but a
	major version may redefine it; re-derive raw values across major
	upgrades.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- Follow <LinkCard title="Working with positions" href="/guides/working-with-positions/" /> for construction and conversion recipes.
- Check <LinkCard title="Errors" href="/reference/errors/" /> for the error variants named in the limits table.
- Read <LinkCard title="Why Sourcier exists" href="/explanation/why-sourcier/" /> for the reasoning behind packing spans into `u64`s.


---

---
title: Your first source map
description: Register source files, assign stable ids, pack a span into a single u64 and extract the exact bytes it covers.
type: tutorial
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This tutorial walks you through the golden path of Sourcier: registering two
source files, finalizing the map, looking files up by path and id, packing a
span into a single `u64`, and extracting the exact bytes that span covers.
You need Rust 1.99 or later and a terminal. The whole tutorial takes about ten
minutes.

## Prerequisites

- Rust 1.99+ installed through [rustup](https://rustup.rs). Check yours with
  `rustc --version`.
- A terminal with `cargo` on your `PATH`.

## Create a demo project

<Steps>
1. Create a new binary crate and enter it:

	<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo new span-demo
cd span-demo`} />

2. Add Sourcier as a dependency:

	<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo add sourcier`} />

	Cargo adds the current `2.0` release to `Cargo.toml`.

3. Replace the contents of `src/main.rs` with the code from the next step.
</Steps>

## Register files and finalize

Sourcier uses a two-phase lifecycle: you register files first, then call
`finalize()` to sort them, deduplicate registrations and assign stable
one-based ids.

Add this code to `src/main.rs`:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use sourcier::SourceFilesMap;

fn main() {
    // u8 ids support up to 255 files; u16 supports 65,535.
    let mut files = SourceFilesMap::<u8>::new();

    files
        .add_file("src/main.rs", b"fn main() {\\n    println!(\\"Hello\\");\\n}")
        .expect("capacity available");
    files
        .add_file("src/lib.rs", b"pub mod utils;")
        .expect("capacity available");

    // Sorts by path, deduplicates, assigns one-based ids.
    files.finalize().expect("no capacity issue");

    println!("registered {} files", files.len());
}`} />

Run the program:

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo run`} />

You see the expected output:

<Code lang="ansi" code={`registered 2 files`} />

<Aside type="note">
	`add_file` accepts any `impl AsRef<str>` for the path and
	`impl Into<Vec<u8>>` for the content, so you can pass `&str` paths and
	either byte slices or owned buffers.
</Aside>

## Look up files by path and id

After finalization, the map answers queries in constant time. Extend `main`:

<Code lang="rust" code={`// Path to id, and id back to path.
let id = files.get_id("src/main.rs").expect("file present");
assert_eq!(files.get_path(id), Some("src/main.rs"));

// Ids are assigned in sorted path order, starting at 1.
assert_eq!(id, 1);

// Id to full borrowed entry.
let entry = files.get(id).expect("file present");
assert_eq!(entry.path, "src/main.rs");
assert!(entry.content.starts_with(b"fn main"));`} />

`src/lib.rs` sorts before `src/main.rs`, so it receives id `1` and
`src/main.rs` receives id `2`. Sorted ids are stable: the same set of files
always produces the same ids, which makes them safe to persist.

## Pack a span into a u64

`AbsolutePosition` packs five fields — file id, start line, start column, end
line and end column — into one `u64`. Lines and columns are one-based and the
end is inclusive:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use sourcier::{AbsolutePosition, SourceFilePosition};

let pos = AbsolutePosition::new(id, 2, 5, 2, 22);

assert_eq!(pos.file_id(), id);
assert_eq!(pos.start_line(), 2);
assert_eq!(pos.start_column(), 5);
assert_eq!(pos.end_line(), 2);
assert_eq!(pos.end_column(), 22);`} />

`AbsolutePosition::new` is infallible and zero-cost: values are encoded as-is.
Use `try_new` when you want the span validated as a well-formed, one-based
region:

<Code lang="rust" code={`assert!(AbsolutePosition::<u8>::try_new(1, 2, 1, 1, 1).is_err());
assert!(AbsolutePosition::<u8>::try_new(1, 1, 1, 1, 1).is_ok());`} />

## Extract the exact bytes of the span

With the default `view` feature, the map bridges positions back to the bytes
they cover:

<Code lang="rust" code={`assert_eq!(
    files.view(id, &pos),
    Some(&b"println!(\\"Hello\\");"[..])
);`} />

`view` returns the bytes of the span including any line terminators it
covers. For UTF-8 source you can use `view_str`, which returns `&str` and
yields `None` when the span cuts a multi-byte character.

Your program now registers files, looks them up, packs positions and extracts
source bytes. Print the extracted view at the end of `main` to see it in
action:

<Code lang="rust" code={`if let Some(bytes) = files.view(id, &pos) {
    println!("{}", String::from_utf8_lossy(bytes));
}`} />

<Code lang="ansi" code={`println!("Hello");`} />
